formalDefinition: {(x,y,k) | x and y are strings, k is int, and there exists a sequence of k operations to transform x into y}
problemDefinition: Find the minimum number of operations (insertion, deletion, substitution) required to transform one string into another.
outputDescription: The minimum number of single-character edit operations required to transform x into y
source: Arturs Backurs and P. Indyk, “Edit Distance Cannot Be Computed in Strongly Subquadratic Time (unless SETH is false),” DSpace@MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology), Jun. 2015
instanceFormat: Format: {(x,y) | x is string, y is string} A string containing a comma, quote, or leading/trailing space is written in double quotes, with \" for a quote and \ for a backslash, e.g. ("a,b", c). An optional third field k (an integer) is accepted and ignored. Example: (horse, ros)
certificateFormat: Format: k | minimum number of single-character edit operations (insert, delete, substitute) to transform x into y Example: 3

defaultSolver.solverDefinition: Finds the edit distance between two strings using dynamic programming.
defaultSolver.source: R. A. Wagner and M. J. Fischer, “The String-to-String Correction Problem,” Journal of the ACM, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 168-173, Jan. 1974

defaultVerifier.verifierDefinition: Verifies that a proposed edit distance is correct for the input strings.

defaultVisualization.visualizationDefinition: Draws the dynamic-programming grid, x down the side and y across the top. Each cell is the cost of turning a prefix of x into a prefix of y, worked out from the three cells before it; the cheapest path back from the corner spells out the edits.

solver.solverDefinition: Finds the edit distance between two strings using dynamic programming.
solver.source: R. A. Wagner and M. J. Fischer, “The String-to-String Correction Problem,” Journal of the ACM, vol. 21, no. 1, pp. 168-173, Jan. 1974
